title: ZVOL data corruption with zvol_use_blk_mq=1
body: I am running Arch Linux with kernel 6.6.0-rc4 and the zfs-2.2-release branch plus Linux 6.6 compatibility patches. Installing Ubuntu 23.10 with virt-manager onto a sparse, compressed ZVOL produces a VM that cannot boot after installation. The libvirt disk uses the raw ZVOL with native I/O, discard="unmap", and a reported physical block size of 16384. A raw image works correctly. With zvol_use_blk_mq=1 the ZVOL-backed installation is unbootable, while zvol_use_blk_mq=0 works flawlessly.

symptoms_visible: After I install Ubuntu 23.10 onto the ZVOL with zvol_use_blk_mq=1, the VM cannot boot.
The same installation works with raw-image storage, and the ZVOL works flawlessly when I use zvol_use_blk_mq=0.
N0.label: N0 blk-mq ZVOL boot failure reported

symptoms_visible: The ZVOL has a 16K volblocksize, matching the configured 16K physical block size, but the VM still cannot boot with zvol_use_blk_mq=1.
Removing the physical_block_size setting or using BIOS instead of UEFI does not change the boot failure.
N1.label: N1 block-size and firmware alternatives checked

symptoms_visible: The VM remains unbootable with blk-mq enabled whether the guest reports a 16384-byte or 512-byte physical block size.
N2.label: N2 guest and host sector details collected

symptoms_visible: With the linked candidate fix applied on my system, the ZVOL-backed VM installs and boots successfully.
N3.label: N3 candidate fix verified by reporter

symptoms_visible: The Ubuntu VM stored on the ZVOL installs and boots correctly with blk-mq enabled on a build containing the tested fix.
N_terminal.label: terminal blk-mq read fix resolved boot failure

question_patterns: What does zfs get volblocksize report for the affected ZVOL?
Can you check the actual volblocksize of the volume?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: My output shows volblocksize=16K with source default. The parent filesystem has recordsize=128K, but the ZVOL itself was created with the new 16K default.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The ZVOL actually has an unusual volblocksize that does not match the value advertised to the guest, and matching the two makes the VM boot.
The ZVOL reports 16K as a locally configured value rather than as the default.

question_patterns: Can you remove the physical_block_size declaration and retry the installation?
Does the failure still occur when libvirt is allowed to use its default block-size reporting?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. I removed the physical_block_size line and the installed system was still unbootable with zvol_use_blk_mq=1.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Removing the physical_block_size declaration makes the installed VM boot normally with zvol_use_blk_mq=1.

edges.comment: Issue comments c0-c6 and c9 describe the reporter's affected Arch system. The actual 16K volblocksize, the unchanged failure after omitting the libvirt block-size declaration, and the BIOS test rule out the opening sector-size and UEFI theories without importing any other participant's deployment.

question_patterns: What does the guest report for hw_sector_size and physical_block_size with and without the libvirt block-size setting?
Can you read the virtual disk's sector sizes from sysfs in both configurations?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With the physical_block_size setting, /sys/class/block/vda/queue/{hw_sector_size,physical_block_size} prints 512 and 16384. Without it, the same files print 512 and 512.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The guest reports an invalid or unexpected sector size only in the failing configuration, and changing it makes the VM boot.
The guest reports 512/16384 with the setting and 512/4096 without it, but both configurations still fail only with blk-mq enabled.

question_patterns: Is the pool backed by real disks or file-based vdevs?
What storage device backs the pool, and what logical block size does it use?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The pool is backed by a single 4 TB WD Black SN850X NVMe drive, formatted with a 4K logical block address size instead of the default 512 bytes.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The pool is on a different model of 4K-LBA NVMe drive, with the same blk-mq-only behavior.

edges.comment: Issue comments c12-c16: participant2 asks for the guest-visible sector sizes and pool backing, and the reporter supplies outputs from the same affected setup. The unrelated Debian/QEMU problem raised in c19 is deliberately excluded from this chain.

question_patterns: Can you apply the linked candidate change and retry the install and boot on your system?
Please test the proposed patch on the affected host and tell me whether the VM boots.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I confirm it works on my system, thanks!

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The VM is still unbootable after I apply the linked candidate change.
The installation and boot both work with the linked candidate change, but I tested a different Ubuntu 23.10 snapshot.

edges.comment: Issue comments c21-c22: participant2 asks the original reporter to test the linked candidate fix, and the reporter confirms it works. This is pre-landing candidate verification and therefore remains a measurement clarification.

solution.intent: Use and ship the reporter-verified correction to the ZVOL blk-mq path so reads return the installed data correctly; until that correction is available, disable zvol_use_blk_mq at pool import rather than changing guest block sizes or reinstalling the VM.
solution.concrete_example: Apply the linked, reporter-tested blk-mq correction and retest the ZVOL-backed VM. On an affected unpatched build, export the pool, set zvol_use_blk_mq=0, and re-import it to use the old BIO path until a build containing the correction is installed.
solution.inference_hint: Participant2 independently reproduced the failure on a brd-backed pool, found matching MBR and partition metadata, and later observed that a ZVOL installed under blk-mq booted after changing the active path across pool re-imports. The engineer concluded that the installed writes were correct and reads through the blk-mq path were wrong. That read-versus-write diagnosis is engineer-side inference, not something the reporter produced.

edges.comment: Technical resolution from c17-c22: participant2 reproduces the original problem independently, narrows it to reads through the blk-mq path, proposes a linked fix, and the original reporter verifies that fix on the affected system. Comments c23-c28 concern a later TrueNAS deployment that participant5 ultimately treats as a separate issue; only c24's general import-time workaround is retained.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause as a defect in the ZVOL blk-mq read path: data written during installation is read back incorrectly through that path, rather than the guest installation necessarily having been written corruptly.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the blk-mq on/off comparison, the unchanged failure with both guest physical-block-size reports, the independently reproduced behavior, and the reporter's successful test of the candidate correction.
Must not settle on a 16K volblocksize mismatch, the libvirt physical_block_size declaration, or UEFI as the cause; the ZVOL was 16K, omission of the declaration still failed, and BIOS also failed.
The durable resolution is a build containing the tested ZVOL blk-mq correction. Disabling zvol_use_blk_mq at pool import is acceptable only as a temporary workaround for an unpatched build.
Must have the affected reporter verify installation and boot on a build containing the correction before declaring the problem resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical Linux and ZFS user who can build a release branch with compatibility patches, configure libvirt XML, inspect ZFS properties and sysfs sector sizes, change module parameters, and test a proposed source patch.
persona_hint.communication_style: Direct, evidence-driven, and technically detailed; challenges speculative explanations with controlled comparisons and pasted command output, while responding promptly to focused test requests.
